listeningScripts.title: Airline Baggage Delay
listeningScripts.text: Passenger: Excuse me, my baggage didn't arrive on my flight from Vancouver. Airline Agent: I'm very sorry to hear that. Let me help you file a report. What is your confirmation number? Passenger: It's VH-4829. I arrived about an hour ago on flight AC-127. Agent: Got it. Did you check your bag through to your final destination or pick it up here in Calgary? Passenger: I checked it all the way to Calgary. I have the baggage claim ticket right here. Agent: Perfect. Can I see that? The tag number is LM-58493. Your bag is a black Samsonite roller, correct? Passenger: Yes, that's right. It has a red ribbon on the handle. Agent: Great. I've found it in the system. It actually came off the plane but was misrouted to Edmonton by mistake. It's on the next flight back to Calgary, which arrives at 6:15 PM tonight. Passenger: So I'll have it this evening? Agent: Yes, we'll have it delivered to your hotel by 8 PM. Where are you staying? Passenger: The Fairmont Palliser downtown. What compensation will I get? Agent: Because the delay is less than 24 hours and the bag will be delivered today, we'll provide a $50 travel voucher for your next flight with us.

listeningScripts.title: Fitness Class Enrollment
listeningScripts.text: Trainer: Welcome to the studio. Is this your first class? Maya: Yeah, I'm pretty nervous. Trainer: Don't worry, everyone starts somewhere. What's your experience with yoga? Maya: I've done some stretching at home, but never a full class like this. Trainer: That's great. Let's get you set up. We have mats over there, and grab a water bottle from the cooler. Maya: How long is the class? Trainer: It's 60 minutes total. We start with breathing exercises, warm up, then move through poses, and end with meditation. Maya: That sounds good. What's the hardest part for beginners? Trainer: Usually it's learning to listen to your body. Don't push too hard too fast. If something hurts, modify it or take a break. Maya: Good to know. How many classes should I take per week to see results? Trainer: For best results, aim for three times a week. Even once a week is great though. Maya: I'll start with twice a week and see how it goes. Trainer: Perfect. That's a solid plan. Let's get started.

listeningScripts.title: University Orientation: First Week Checklist
listeningScripts.text: Hello, welcome to orientation week. I'm here to walk you through essential tasks for your first week. First, attend your faculty's orientation meeting on Monday at ten AM in the Student Centre. Bring your student ID. Second, register for your courses online by Wednesday, August 28th. Early registration means better class times. Third, purchase your textbooks from the university bookstore before classes start. Fourth, get your student photo ID taken at the Services Office between 9 and 4 on any day this week. The photo ID is required for library access and residence entry. Fifth, activate your email account at the IT support desk. Your email is your primary communication channel for all university announcements. Sixth, find your classes on a campus map. Most buildings are located around the central quad. Seventh, attend the Welcome Social on Friday evening in the gymnasium. It's a great way to meet other students and faculty. Eighth, complete your health and immunization form at Student Health Services. This is mandatory before attending classes. Finally, budget about three hundred dollars for books and materials. Questions? Visit the information desk in the main foyer.

listeningScripts.title: New Brunswick Fisheries Management Plan
listeningScripts.text: New Brunswick has introduced a comprehensive fisheries management plan aimed at rebuilding declining fish stocks and supporting the province's fishing communities. The plan allocates 67 million dollars over five years to research, enforcement, and sustainable fishing initiatives. Atlantic salmon populations have declined by 48 percent over the past two decades, prompting urgent action. The plan imposes stricter catch limits on cod and halibut in designated zones. Fishing vessel owners participating in conservation programs receive subsidies up to 200,000 dollars for upgrading to eco-friendly equipment. The program mandates trap modifications to reduce unintended marine mammal bycatch by 35 percent. Over 3,200 fishermen and their families depend on this industry in New Brunswick. The province is establishing a new fisheries research center employing 120 marine scientists. Marine Protected Areas will expand to cover an additional 8 percent of provincial waters. The plan aims to achieve sustainable fish stock levels by 2032.

listeningScripts.title: University Program Expansion Planning
listeningScripts.text:
Dean Robert: We've been asked to consider expanding our engineering program, particularly in renewable energy studies. The faculty has requested three additional full-time instructors and funding for new laboratory equipment. The cost would be approximately 2.4 million dollars over two years. Given our current budget constraints, I'm hesitant to commit to this expansion.

Professor Elena: I understand the budget concerns, Dean, but we're actually losing enrollment to competing universities who offer these programs. Last year, we lost 150 potential engineering students to schools with stronger renewable energy options. If we don't expand now, we'll fall behind. Plus, there's significant industry demand for graduates with renewable energy expertise. Companies are specifically recruiting from universities with these specialized programs.

Student Representative Malik: From a student perspective, I absolutely support this expansion. Many of my classmates are interested in sustainability and green technology, but we don't have the courses or facilities to support that focus. I think this investment would make our university much more attractive to prospective students, which would actually increase our overall enrollment and revenue.

Budget Committee Member Diana: Malik makes a good point about revenue. If this program attracts even 200 additional students, the tuition revenue would exceed the expansion costs within three years. And we could explore partnerships with industry for funding. I've been in conversations with several renewable energy companies that might contribute equipment or funding in exchange for access to our graduates for recruitment.

listeningScripts.title: Mental Health Parity in Insurance Coverage
listeningScripts.text: Mental health needs to be treated with the same importance as physical health in our insurance system. We talk about mental health awareness, but when it comes to actual coverage, it's dramatically underfunded. Most insurance plans cover mental health at lower rates than physical health. If you have a broken arm, insurance covers months of physical therapy. If you have depression or anxiety, you get maybe 10 sessions of therapy a year, and psychologist visits might only be 50 percent covered. This creates barriers. Many people avoid treatment because they can't afford it, and their conditions worsen. The economic impact is massive. Mental health issues cost the economy 51 billion dollars annually in Canada through lost productivity, emergency services, and hospitalizations. Yet we invest a fraction of that in prevention and treatment. Here's what frustrates me most: we have effective treatments. Therapy works. Medication helps. But access is limited by insurance coverage. A person struggling with bipolar disorder shouldn't have to choose between therapy and rent. Insurance companies argue coverage limits are necessary for cost control, but that's shortsighted. When people get mental health treatment early, they use fewer emergency services, work more, and contribute to society. The ROI on mental health coverage is actually positive. I'm advocating for mandatory parity—insurance companies should cover mental health at the same level as physical health. This means removing visit limits, lowering copayments, and covering evidence-based treatments. It's not just compassionate; it's economically smart.
